cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T4 and T5 answer each other directly on whether money can buy back time.
cells.limitation: T1-T3 are parallel openings; Stoic T3 and T6 never engage the money argument.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T5 introduces outsourceable versus non-outsourceable losses; T7 builds its concession on it.
cells.limitation: Only one distinction develops; the Stoic adaptation claim (T3) never advances past its opening.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T4-T5 examine whether higher pay can offset lost time.
cells.limitation: Commute mode, current commute and career growth never raised; adaptation versus cost never actually debated.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian revises his calculus in light of the Essentialist's T5 point.
cells.limitation: The Stoic stays isolated; no mind reshapes or is reshaped by his view.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D sharpens the question to manageable challenge versus degradation of life.
cells.limitation: Section D's main disagreement was never argued between minds in the debate.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T4 states the Essentialist's premise accurately: time treated as the primary metric.
cells.limitation: T6 recasts T5's point about non-outsourceable presence as rest being required for a good life.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T4 names the assumption that time is primary and what breaks if false; T5 answers.
cells.limitation: Nobody challenges the Stoic's T3 and T6 claim that the user can simply adapt.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T1's fifteen hours weekly checks: 90 min x 2 x 5 days = 15 h.
cells.limitation: T3 voices Milton's 'mind is its own place' as Marcus Aurelius (suspected misattribution).

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T3 offers the fear of a disturbed peace as a guess, not a fact.
cells.limitation: Section E overstates: commuting costs alone would not reveal the true net gain.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T7 drops the simple-sum claim, crediting the Essentialist's T5 point.
cells.limitation: The Stoic never concedes anything or is pressed to; T9 does not answer T6.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern, including ambiguity about what the user is really asking
cells.example: Section D frames the question as challenge versus degradation of quality of life.
cells.limitation: Never asks what the three daily hours would displace for this user.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T1 converts the 90-minute commute into fifteen weekly hours.
cells.limitation: The 25 percent figure is never converted into anything the argument uses.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: Section E ties the choice to whether money or autonomy matters more.
cells.limitation: User priorities never asked; T6 substitutes the Stoic's value of character forged by endurance.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: Section E names commuting costs as eating into the raise.
cells.limitation: Commute mode (driving versus usable train time) never considered, though it changes the cost.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on precarious versus stable finances.
cells.limitation: Current commute, remote options, transport mode and dependants never asked or branched.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: T3 tentatively offers fear of lost peace as a motive.
cells.limitation: Only one motive offered; no alternatives or question the user could answer.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T4-T5 surface the assumption that money can buy back time.
cells.limitation: Assumptions examined are the speakers'; the user's own, like raise equals gain, barely touched.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T5 contrasts salary with rest and presence with family.
cells.limitation: Values conflict stays generic money versus time in Section E.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T9 names burnout risk clouding judgment about resilience.
cells.limitation: Obligation, family expectation or career pressure behind the offer never explored.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: Section E gives conditions the user can apply to themselves.
cells.limitation: Almost no questions handed to the user; T6 tells them what forges character.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options, including waiting, learning more, or a limited step
cells.example: Section E frames accept versus decline by financial situation.
cells.limitation: Negotiating hybrid work, relocation or a counteroffer never appear as options.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs in terms that matter to the user; no option treated as costless
cells.example: T1 weighs pay against fifteen weekly hours; T9 prices the trial's burnout cost.
cells.limitation: Declining is treated as costless; forgone career growth never mentioned.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: compute how much of the raise commuting costs consume.
cells.limitation: No threshold says which net-gain result favours accepting or declining; T8's one week ungrounded.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section D names whether the user can adapt as the open unknown.
cells.limitation: Unknowns are not ranked; commute mode and flexibility left unmentioned.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps that follow from the analysis and fit the constraints
cells.example: Section E's commuting-cost calculation is cheap and follows from the analysis.
cells.limitation: T8's three-hour daily trial is costly, as T9 itself concedes.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T5 and T8 use plain, concrete wording.
cells.limitation: T1's felicific calculus is left unexplained.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T4, T5 and T6 name the mind they answer.
cells.limitation: T9's 'respects your constraint of time' points to no identifiable turn or claim.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Nine turns, all within the word range, easy to follow.
cells.limitation: Uniformly short turns leave each claim one sentence deep.

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices, with explicit changes of position
cells.example: Positions differ: calculus (T1), essential trade-off (T2), inner control (T3).
cells.limitation: One shared hedging register across all minds; might and perhaps throughout.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: No turn repeats another verbatim; the debate is compact.
cells.limitation: T4-T6 open by restating the prior speaker's claim before answering.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension arising from the issue itself
cells.example: T5 raises presence with family as something salary cannot buy.
cells.limitation: Stakes stay abstract; no concrete day of the user's life is pictured.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals that stay plausible. ★ A reversal the text traces to an earlier turn's argument, naming what changed the speaker's mind. A change of position with no stated cause is a template, not a reversal
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian abandons his calculus, naming T5's non-outsourceable losses as cause.
cells.limitation: The concession is total and flat, with no struggle before it.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice without caricature
cells.example: T6 Stoic's character forged by endurance has some flavour.
cells.limitation: All three minds speak in one hedged, neutral register.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T4's money buying back time is the one sharp turn.
cells.limitation: No analogy or vivid example; T3's best line is borrowed from Milton.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement, with varied rhythm rather than constant intensity
cells.example: T9 adds a late twist by pricing the trial itself.
cells.limitation: Uniform rhythm; the debate ends on a minor point without build.

strengths: T4-T5 exchange genuinely tests whether money can buy back time, and T7 revises on it.
T7 Utilitarian reversal is caused, crediting the Essentialist's T5 argument.
Section E's commuting-cost calculation is a concrete, cheap step the user can run.
weaknesses: Consequential facts (commute mode, current commute, remote options) never asked or branched (Sections D-E).
The Stoic's adapt-inwardly claim (T3, T6) is never challenged, yet Section D calls it the main disagreement.
All three minds share one hedged register, flattening voice and drama throughout.

symptoms.observed: No turn asks about commute mode, current commute, remote work or dependants.
symptoms.evidence: If your current financial situation is precarious

symptoms.observed: Options stay accept or decline; negotiating hybrid work never appears.
symptoms.evidence: try a one-week experiment where you wake up

symptoms.observed: The Stoic's adaptation claim draws no objection from either other mind.
symptoms.evidence: you might find tranquility even in a long journey

symptoms.observed: Every mind hedges with might or perhaps in the same register.
symptoms.evidence: the net pleasure might actually increase

symptoms.observed: Commuting-cost step gives no threshold; trial length not drawn from user facts.
symptoms.evidence: calculate exactly how much of that 25 percent increase

findings.description: The mind is its own place is Milton's Paradise Lost phrasing, voiced as the Meditations-based Stoic without quotation marks.
Claims commuting costs will reveal the true net gain, ignoring the time cost the debate centred on.

rubric_fit_notes: The user's question is about how to decide, so method-level answers are apt; personal details are sparse, which limits C3 ceilings somewhat, though the debate also asked nothing.
